title: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails
description_short: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails
description_medium: In August 2016, Roger Stone told Donald Trump and campaign officials that WikiLeaks was expected to publish emails from Hillary Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta. A Senate Intelligence Committee report later confirmed that Stone passed along the information, but could not determine how much was genuine advance knowledge or where it came from. The report also described Stone and Jerome Corsi discussing an explanation and deleting communications.
description_long:
In early August 2016, Roger Stone learned that WikiLeaks planned to release emails from John Podesta, chairman of Hillary Clinton’s campaign, and relayed that expectation to Donald Trump and campaign officials. The Senate Intelligence Committee later confirmed that the information reached Trump, Paul Manafort, Rick Gates, and likely others. Investigators could not establish how much of Stone’s information was authentic or nonpublic, or identify its source.

Jerome Corsi, whom Stone was believed to have relied on, gave conflicting accounts of whether he had received a tip or inferred that Podesta was the target. The committee described Corsi and Stone coordinating an explanation and Corsi deleting related communications. On October 7, Stone asked WikiLeaks to release the emails as a distraction from the Access Hollywood recording. The report establishes that campaign figures received advance word and that Stone sought a release; it leaves unresolved what Trump and others knew about the source and timing.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump learns that WikiLeaks has Clinton campaign emails

title: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views
description_short: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views
description_medium: A Center for Countering Digital Hate report counted 17.1 billion views for Elon Musk’s political posts on X between his July 13, 2024 endorsement of Donald Trump and Election Day. The group said the total exceeded twice the views recorded for political campaign ads in X’s disclosure data over the same period. The comparison measures reported views, not unique viewers or the posts’ effect on votes.
description_long:
The Center for Countering Digital Hate reported that Elon Musk’s political posts on X received 17.1 billion views between his July 13, 2024 endorsement of Donald Trump and the election. The group described many of the posts as false or misleading and compared the view count with X’s disclosure data for political campaign advertisements, which recorded less than half as many views over the same period.

The comparison puts Musk’s organic posts alongside paid ads to illustrate their reported reach on the platform during a presidential campaign. A view count does not show how many distinct people saw the posts, whether they believed them, or whether the posts changed anyone’s vote. The report’s central finding is the scale of exposure it attributed to Musk’s political content in the months before the 2024 election; it does not measure persuasion or electoral impact.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: REPORT: Elon Musk's political propaganda earned 17 billion views

title: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama
description_short: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama
description_medium: Donald Trump announced on September 2, 2025, that U.S. Space Command headquarters would move from Colorado to Alabama. Colorado’s congressional delegation warned that relocation could delay readiness and cost public money; a Pentagon inspector general had also identified readiness risks. Trump criticized Colorado’s mail-voting system around the same time. The timeline interpreted the move as political retaliation, while Trump denied that political support drove the decision.
description_long:
On September 2, 2025, Donald Trump announced that U.S. Space Command headquarters would move from Colorado to Alabama. Colorado’s congressional delegation, including four Republicans, criticized the decision, warning of delays to space-defense readiness, unnecessary expense, and strategic risk. A Pentagon inspector general had previously identified readiness concerns related to relocation.

The move was expected to take three to four years, require about 1,700 personnel to relocate, and cost hundreds of millions of dollars. The report also cited an estimated long-term cost advantage of $426 million for Huntsville, a saving that would take time to realize. Trump separately attacked Colorado’s mail-voting system. The timeline characterized the relocation as punishment for Colorado’s voting record and a reward for Alabama’s support; Trump denied that political support influenced his choice. The announcement set off a dispute over strategy, cost, and motive, while leaving the practical case for the move unresolved.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Punishing Colorado, Trump moves Space Command HQ to Alabama

title: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein
description_short: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein
description_medium: Les Wexner transferred his Manhattan townhouse at 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein in 1995 or earlier, according to the timeline; the exact date is unknown. The transfer became public in a January 1996 New York Times report. Wexner had bought the seven-story home in 1989 for $13.2 million and spent tens of millions on renovations and furnishings. Epstein later confirmed that the property was his.
description_long:
Les Wexner bought the seven-story townhouse at 9 East 71st Street in Manhattan in 1989 for $13.2 million. He later spent tens of millions of dollars on renovations, art, and furnishings. The New York Times reported in January 1996 that Jeffrey Epstein had become the owner; the timeline places the transfer in 1995 or earlier but says the exact date is unknown.

The newspaper described Epstein as Wexner’s protégé and one of his financial advisers. Asked about the house, Epstein said it was now his and that Wexner had rarely stayed there. The report described elaborate features, including a concealed reinforced bathroom and a heated sidewalk, which conveyed the scale of the residence but did not explain the legal terms of the transfer. The available account documents a major property transfer and the financial relationship between the two men. It does not connect Donald Trump to the transaction.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Les Wexner gives 9 East 71st Street to Jeffrey Epstein

title: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020
description_short: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020
description_medium: On September 7, 2020, Jack Posobiec posted about “Stop The Steal 2020,” while Ali Alexander told a Periscope audience he was building a digital campaign around the slogan. Alexander described a database and alert system for Trump supporters near election offices, ballot-counting sites, and court proceedings. Pro-Trump Facebook pages began using the phrase hours later, but the timeline could not establish who operated them.
description_long:
On September 7, 2020, Jack Posobiec tweeted about “Stop The Steal 2020.” Ali Alexander separately told viewers on Periscope that he was building a digital campaign to “stop the steal.” Alexander said the effort would collect information about Trump supporters and map sites in swing states where ballots were counted or election officials worked. He described collecting cellphone numbers so people within 100 miles could be alerted to locations he considered involved in improper counting or to federal court hearings. He later released a website and app for the database.

Pro-Trump Facebook pages began using “Stop The Steal” within hours, but the timeline says they may have been run by Alexander, Posobiec, or others. The posts and announcements document plans to organize supporters around election-related locations. They do not show how many people joined, whether alerts were sent, or what happened at any election office as a result.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Jack Posobiec and Ali Alexander announce Stop The Steal 2020

title: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe
description_short: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe
description_medium: A private Signal conversation on March 14, 2025, included White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller discussing U.S. strikes on Yemen’s Houthi movement. Miller wrote that Donald Trump had approved the strikes and argued that the United States should seek economic returns from Europe and Egypt. He also asked how a contribution could be enforced if Europe refused. The messages show a proposed rationale, not an implemented payment arrangement.
description_long:
In a private Signal conversation on March 14, 2025, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller discussed U.S. strikes on Yemen’s Houthi movement with administration officials. Miller wrote that Donald Trump had given a “green light” and argued that the United States should make clear what it expected from Egypt and Europe in return. He asked how the administration could enforce a requirement if Europe did not pay, adding that the United States needed further economic gain after restoring freedom of navigation.

The conversation took place amid Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, which had prompted commercial and military vessels to take longer routes. Signal was not authorized for confidential government communications. Miller’s messages framed military action as potential leverage over countries that would benefit from safer passage. They document a proposal discussed inside the administration, not an adopted policy: the messages do not show that any payment deal or enforcement mechanism was put in place.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Miller: Trump needs Houthi strike to extort Egypt & Europe

title: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge
description_short: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge
description_medium: In March 2017, the Trump administration demanded the immediate resignation of all 46 U.S. attorneys appointed under Barack Obama. Preet Bharara, whom Trump had asked to stay, was dismissed after refusing to leave. The abrupt request came while federal investigations and prosecutions were active. Legal experts described gradual transitions as customary, prompting concern that the mass departures could disrupt law enforcement and invite political influence.
description_long:
On March 10, 2017, the Trump administration demanded the immediate resignation of all 46 U.S. attorneys appointed under Barack Obama. Preet Bharara was among them. The supplied account says Trump had personally asked Bharara to stay, but Bharara refused a White House phone call and was dismissed. The timing drew attention because federal investigations and prosecutions were ongoing.

Legal experts described gradual replacement of U.S. attorneys as the customary way for a new administration to maintain continuity in federal law enforcement. Bharara’s investigations involving Trump allies and associates added to questions about political motivation, although the episode was not adjudicated as a case of improper motive. The mass demand put pressure on the normal transition between administrations and raised concerns about continuity and prosecutorial independence. It also tested the boundary between a president’s authority to appoint prosecutors and the expectation that enforcement decisions remain free from personal or partisan direction.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Fires All 46 U.S. Attorneys Overnight — Unprecedented Political Purge

title: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister
description_short: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister
description_medium: In a 2018 interview at Jeffrey Epstein’s New York home, journalist James B. Stewart asked about reports that Epstein was helping Tesla find a chairman after an SEC investigation. Epstein claimed he had worked with Elon Musk and Tesla and discussed investment with Saudi Arabia. Musk and Tesla denied contact. Stewart’s account does not verify Epstein’s claims; he also said he could not confirm whether later dinner invitations involving Epstein took place.
description_long:
New York Times journalist James B. Stewart interviewed Jeffrey Epstein at his Manhattan home in 2018. Epstein claimed he had been working with Elon Musk and Tesla, amid reports that he was helping the company find a chairman after an SEC investigation. He told Stewart Tesla would not confirm their contact because he was “radioactive,” and said he was discussing investment with Saudi Arabia. Musk and Tesla denied ever contacting Epstein, and Stewart’s account did not independently verify Epstein’s claim.

Epstein also said he might become a minister and described how people could use him as a confidant. During the interview he made comments minimizing sex with underage girls. Stewart later received dinner invitations involving Epstein and public figures but said he could not confirm whether the dinners occurred. The account records what Epstein claimed and the denials that followed; it does not establish that he performed business work for Tesla or secured Saudi investment.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Epstein says he's working with Tesla, wants to become a minister

title: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack
description_short: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack
description_medium: On March 25, 2021, seven House committees asked 16 federal agencies for records about the government’s preparation for and response to the January 6 Capitol attack. The requests covered the White House, Justice Department, FBI, Pentagon, National Guard, and other agencies. The inquiry followed the failure to reach bipartisan agreement on an independent commission. The letters began an investigation; they were not findings about the administration’s responsibility.
description_long:
On March 25, 2021, seven House committees sent records requests to 16 federal agencies about the government’s preparations for and response to the January 6 attack on the Capitol. The review sought communications dating back to December 1 and covered decisions made during the final weeks of the Trump administration. Requests went to the White House, National Archives, Justice Department, FBI, Pentagon, National Guard, Homeland Security, Interior Department, U.S. Park Police, and intelligence agencies, among others.

The inquiry came after Speaker Nancy Pelosi was unable to secure bipartisan cooperation for an independent commission. At the time, federal prosecutors had charged more than 300 people in connection with the breach, including some accused of conspiring to stop Electoral College certification. The committees’ letters sought information and preservation of records; they did not constitute a completed investigation or determine the administration’s responsibility. They marked an effort by Congress to reconstruct what agencies knew and did before and during the attack.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: House launches formal investigation into Trump Admin & the Capitol attack

title: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies
description_short: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump halted new offshore wind leasing in federal waters and directed agencies to review existing leases. He also sought to claw back clean-energy subsidies authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act. The supplied account says the directives threatened projects and jobs, and that states and companies challenged them, including on contract grounds. The orders began reviews and legal disputes; they did not immediately cancel every existing lease.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued executive orders halting new offshore wind leasing in federal waters and directing agencies to review whether existing leases should be ended. He also sought to claw back clean-energy subsidies authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act. The directives disrupted plans in an industry whose projects depend on federal lease agreements, and the supplied account says tens of thousands of jobs were at risk.

States and companies challenged the actions, arguing that ending leases or related arrangements could violate contractual commitments. Those lawsuits put the government’s obligations at issue, but the available account does not report a final court resolution. The orders marked a shift away from federal support for offshore wind and certain clean-energy incentives. They directed agencies to review existing leases; they did not cancel every lease on the day they were issued. The policy change therefore began with new restrictions and reviews while the scope of lasting cancellations remained under dispute.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Ends Offshore Wind Leases and Terminates Clean Energy Subsidies

title: Trump: Richard Grenell & Kashyap Patel promoted to ODNI to weaken U.S. Intelligence
description_short: Trump: Richard Grenell & Kashyap Patel promoted to ODNI to weaken U.S. Intelligence
description_medium: Donald Trump replaced acting Director of National Intelligence Joseph Maguire with Richard Grenell in February 2020. Grenell, a former ambassador and media commentator, had no prior intelligence-community experience. The administration also moved Kashyap “Kash” Patel from the National Security Council to an advisory role at ODNI. The timeline links Patel to a White House request to reduce the office’s staff, prompting concern about political influence and the agency’s capacity.
description_long:
In February 2020, Donald Trump replaced acting Director of National Intelligence Joseph Maguire with Richard Grenell, who had served as ambassador to Germany and as a media consultant but had no prior intelligence-community experience. The administration also reassigned Kashyap “Kash” Patel from the National Security Council to advise Grenell at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Patel had worked for Representative Devin Nunes and had shared disputed information about Ukraine with Trump. The timeline says he later took part in an ODNI reorganization and a White House request to reduce the office’s staff. The changes put officials seen as close to Trump in senior intelligence roles and raised concern about the independence and capacity of agencies that provide nonpartisan assessments to policymakers. The title characterizes the changes as an effort to weaken U.S. intelligence; the appointments and reported staffing request are documented, but the officials’ motive is not established.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Richard Grenell & Kashyap Patel promoted to ODNI to weaken U.S. Intelligence
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Richard Grenell & Kashyap Patel promoted to ODNI to weaken U.S. Intelligence

title: Trump: ICE abducts first U.S. resident for protesting genocide, more victims to come
description_short: Trump: ICE abducts first U.S. resident for protesting genocide, more victims to come
description_medium: Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Mahmoud Khalil, a Palestinian permanent U.S. resident and Columbia University activist, at his New York home in March 2025. Secretary of State Marco Rubio approved the action under an immigration-law provision concerning foreign-policy consequences. Khalil had helped negotiate between university leaders and students protesting the war in Gaza. A federal judge blocked his immediate deportation, leaving the legal challenge ongoing.
description_long:
In March 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Mahmoud Khalil, a Palestinian permanent U.S. resident and recent Columbia University graduate, at his New York home. Khalil had served as a negotiator between university leaders and students protesting the school’s position on Israel and Gaza. The account says Secretary of State Marco Rubio approved the detention under a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act that permits action when the secretary determines a noncitizen’s presence could have serious foreign-policy consequences. The same law limits restrictions based on lawful beliefs, statements, or associations, subject to a foreign-policy exception.

A federal judge blocked immediate efforts to deport Khalil. The detention brought scrutiny to the use of immigration powers against a permanent resident involved in political protest. Officials made allegations about Khalil’s affiliations, but the account says they did so without evidence. The court’s intervention halted immediate deportation; it did not settle the underlying legal dispute.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: ICE abducts first U.S. resident for protesting genocide, more victims to come
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: ICE abducts first U.S. resident for protesting genocide, more victims to come

title: Trump: Louis DeJoy gives Donald Trump & RNC over $600,000 after USPS job opens
description_short: Trump: Louis DeJoy gives Donald Trump & RNC over $600,000 after USPS job opens
description_medium: Louis DeJoy, then finance chair of the Republican National Committee, gave more than $600,000 to Donald Trump’s campaign and the RNC between October and December 2019. The first donation coincided with the announcement that Postmaster General Megan Brennan would resign. DeJoy became postmaster general in June 2020. He and his wife also held investments in companies connected to the Postal Service, and DeJoy had faced allegations of pressuring employees to donate to Republican campaigns.
description_long:
Between October 16 and December 12, 2019, Louis DeJoy, then the Republican National Committee’s finance chair, gave more than $600,000 to Donald Trump’s campaign and the RNC. The first donation came on the day Postmaster General Megan Brennan announced she would resign. DeJoy became postmaster general in June 2020, before an election expected to rely heavily on mail ballots.

Financial disclosures showed that DeJoy and his wife held substantial investments in companies doing business with or competing against the Postal Service, including XPO Logistics, where DeJoy had been a director. He had also faced allegations that he pressured employees at his former company to contribute to Republican campaigns in exchange for reimbursement. The donations and business interests raised questions about political access, conflicts, and postal oversight. The timing alone does not prove that contributions secured DeJoy’s appointment or that he violated the law as postmaster general.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Louis DeJoy gives Donald Trump & RNC over $600,000 after USPS job opens
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Louis DeJoy gives Donald Trump & RNC over $600,000 after USPS job opens

title: Trump Nominates Alexander Acosta, Architect of Epstein's 2008 Non-Prosecution Agreement, as Labor Secretary
description_short: Trump Nominates Alexander Acosta, Architect of Epstein's 2008 Non-Prosecution Agreement, as Labor Secretary
description_medium: Donald Trump nominated Alexander Acosta to lead the Department of Labor in February 2017. As U.S. attorney in Florida, Acosta had negotiated Jeffrey Epstein’s 2008 non-prosecution agreement. Vicky Ward later reported, through a former White House official, that Acosta said he had been told to leave Epstein alone because Epstein “belonged to intelligence.” That account was described as secondhand or thirdhand and difficult to assess. Acosta resigned in July 2019, the day after Epstein’s federal arrest.
description_long:
Donald Trump nominated Alexander Acosta as Labor Secretary in February 2017. Before joining the cabinet, Acosta had been the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida and negotiated Jeffrey Epstein’s 2008 non-prosecution agreement, which shielded Epstein from federal prosecution under the deal.

Journalist Vicky Ward later reported, based on what a former White House official told her, that Acosta said during transition vetting he had been told to back off Epstein’s case because Epstein “belonged to intelligence.” The account was described as secondhand or thirdhand and difficult to evaluate. No substantiated Justice Department emails supporting the quote have been identified in the supplied correction, so this account does not repeat that claim. Acosta remained Labor Secretary until July 12, 2019, the day after Epstein’s arrest on federal sex-trafficking charges. The nomination raised questions about how Acosta’s role in the Epstein agreement was weighed during vetting; the reported transition remark remains unverified.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Nominates Alexander Acosta, Architect of Epstein's 2008 Non-Prosecution Agreement, as Labor Secretary
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Nominates Alexander Acosta, Architect of Epstein's 2008 Non-Prosecution Agreement, as Labor Secretary

title: DOGE Takes Down Federal Websites Without Authorization — USAID, CDC, Census
description_short: DOGE Takes Down Federal Websites Without Authorization — USAID, CDC, Census
description_medium: In early February 2025, DOGE operatives took control of USAID’s web domain and deactivated about 2,000 employee email accounts, according to the supplied account. The CDC data portal and Census.gov also went offline before being restored. A later DOGE transparency site used a database that outside developers could edit. The incidents disrupted access to federal information and prompted concerns about authorization, security, and safeguards for public data.
description_long:
The supplied account says that in early February 2025, Department of Government Efficiency operatives gained access to USAID’s domain and deactivated roughly 2,000 employee email accounts. It also describes the CDC data portal and Census.gov going offline before both were restored. These events interrupted access to federal websites and agency communications.

In mid-February, DOGE launched a transparency website, doge.gov. Developers found that its database was openly accessible and could be edited from outside the government. The site largely mirrored posts from Elon Musk’s platform, X, despite being presented as an administration transparency tool. Together, the reported incidents raised questions about who authorized changes to agency domains and accounts, how public-facing systems were secured, and whether the new site offered reliable government information. The supplied synopsis characterizes the USAID access as unauthorized, while the linked reporting focuses on security officials being removed after resisting DOGE access to protected systems. The outages and database exposure are reported in the supplied account; their full scope and authorization are not established by that article.

preserved_fields.title: DOGE Takes Down Federal Websites Without Authorization — USAID, CDC, Census
preserved_fields.description_short: DOGE Takes Down Federal Websites Without Authorization — USAID, CDC, Census

title: Trump & friends break federal law again, lie 30+ times at final night of RNC
description_short: Trump & friends break federal law again, lie 30+ times at final night of RNC
description_medium: Donald Trump delivered the Republican National Convention’s closing campaign speech from the White House in August 2020. The linked timeline argued that using federal property for partisan campaigning conflicted with the Hatch Act. It also fact-checked claims from the speech, including Trump’s assertion that the United States had the world’s lowest COVID-19 fatality rate. The event became a nationally televised example of campaign activity at the executive residence.
description_long:
Donald Trump closed the Republican National Convention with a campaign speech from the White House in August 2020. The linked timeline argued that using government property for partisan campaigning conflicted with the Hatch Act, which limits the use of official authority and federal resources to influence elections. The White House had also hosted convention speeches and promotional videos on earlier nights, making the address part of a broader use of the presidential residence for campaign messaging.

The timeline challenged several statements Trump made during the speech. It said his claim that the United States had the lowest COVID-19 fatality rate conflicted with contemporaneous international data. It also examined his remarks on offshoring, energy, police funding, and “Obamagate.” The legal criticism is the source’s characterization; the account does not cite a court ruling adjudicating the convention event as a Hatch Act violation. The speech brought partisan campaigning into an official setting and broadcast contested claims to a national audience.

preserved_fields.title: Trump & friends break federal law again, lie 30+ times at final night of RNC
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump & friends break federal law again, lie 30+ times at final night of RNC

title: Miss Teen USA Contestants Say Trump Entered Dressing Room While Underage Women Were Changing (2001)
description_short: Miss Teen USA Contestants Say Trump Entered Dressing Room While Underage Women Were Changing (2001)
description_medium: After the 2016 release of the Access Hollywood recording, former Miss Teen USA contestants said Donald Trump entered their dressing room during the 2001 pageant while contestants were changing. The pageant included participants aged 14 to 19, and at least four women publicly confirmed the account. One recalled Trump saying, “Don’t worry, ladies, I’ve seen it all before.” Their reports raised concerns about privacy and safeguarding at a pageant for minors.
description_long:
Several former contestants said Donald Trump entered the Miss Teen USA dressing room during the 2001 pageant while participants were changing. The event was held at the Meadowlands Convention Center in New Jersey, and contestants ranged from 14 to 19 years old. At least four women who took part publicly confirmed the account. One recalled Trump looking around the room and saying, “Don’t worry, ladies, I’ve seen it all before.”

The accounts drew renewed attention after the 2016 release of the Access Hollywood tape. In a 2005 interview with Howard Stern, Trump described entering pageant dressing rooms without specifying which pageants he meant. The contestants’ reports raised concerns about adult access, privacy, and safeguarding in a competition that included minors. Their statements are attributed accounts of what they experienced, not a court finding. The description stays with the reported entry and its context, without extending the claims beyond what the former contestants described.

preserved_fields.title: Miss Teen USA Contestants Say Trump Entered Dressing Room While Underage Women Were Changing (2001)
preserved_fields.description_short: Miss Teen USA Contestants Say Trump Entered Dressing Room While Underage Women Were Changing (2001)

title: Canada and Mexico Hit With 25% Tariffs Over Fentanyl Pretext
description_short: Canada and Mexico Hit With 25% Tariffs Over Fentanyl Pretext
description_medium: On February 1, 2025, Donald Trump imposed 25% tariffs on goods from Canada and Mexico, citing fentanyl trafficking and illegal immigration as national emergencies. Leaders in both countries disputed the rationale and announced retaliatory tariffs. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau pointed to U.S. data showing fentanyl seizures at the northern border had fallen near zero. The measures affected trade with the United States’ two largest partners under USMCA and escalated into additional Canadian levies.
description_long:
On February 1, 2025, Donald Trump imposed 25% tariffs on goods from Canada and Mexico, invoking emergency powers and citing fentanyl trafficking and illegal immigration. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called the fentanyl rationale unjustified and pointed to U.S. customs data showing seizures at the northern border had fallen near zero. Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum announced 25% retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods.

Canada announced C$30 billion in counter-tariffs on products including orange juice, wine, beer, coffee, appliances, and motorcycles, then added C$29.8 billion in levies on U.S. steel, aluminum, and autos. Canadian and Chinese officials called the fentanyl justification a pretext for broader protectionism; that was their criticism, not an established finding about Trump’s motive. The measures turned an emergency declaration into a dispute affecting consumer and industrial exports. The episode documents the tariffs and the rapid retaliation, while leaving the economic effects and legal status of the emergency powers unresolved.

preserved_fields.title: Canada and Mexico Hit With 25% Tariffs Over Fentanyl Pretext
preserved_fields.description_short: Canada and Mexico Hit With 25% Tariffs Over Fentanyl Pretext

title: Paris Agreement Withdrawal 2.0: Trump Exits Climate Accord Again on Inauguration Day
description_short: Paris Agreement Withdrawal 2.0: Trump Exits Climate Accord Again on Inauguration Day
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump directed the United States to notify the United Nations of its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and to end or revoke related climate-finance commitments. It was his second withdrawal order; the first was reversed when the Biden administration rejoined in 2021. The decision followed reports that 2024 was the hottest year on record and drew criticism and debate among U.S. allies. The treaty withdrawal would take effect through its formal notice process.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an order directing the United States to notify the United Nations of its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and to stop or revoke related international climate-finance commitments. It began a second withdrawal process: Trump had initiated one during his first term, and Joe Biden rejoined the agreement in 2021. The order directed immediate notification, but withdrawal from the treaty would take effect only after the agreement’s formal notice period.

The decision came as the World Meteorological Organization reported that 2024 was the hottest year on record, about 1.55°C above preindustrial levels. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Europe would continue its climate efforts, and the European Parliament held emergency debates on the geopolitical effects. The order changed U.S. climate diplomacy and financing commitments; it did not itself determine domestic emissions. It renewed uncertainty about the country’s participation in coordinated climate action and support for international climate programs.

preserved_fields.title: Paris Agreement Withdrawal 2.0: Trump Exits Climate Accord Again on Inauguration Day
preserved_fields.description_short: Paris Agreement Withdrawal 2.0: Trump Exits Climate Accord Again on Inauguration Day

title: DOJ Drops Charges Against Hundreds Who Violently Attacked Police on January 6
description_short: DOJ Drops Charges Against Hundreds Who Violently Attacked Police on January 6
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump pardoned people convicted in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack and directed the Justice Department to seek dismissal of unresolved cases. CNN reported that the request covered more than 300 pending cases and that 14 members of far-right groups were released early. Some defendants had been convicted of serious assaults on police. Pardons and dismissal motions ended cases or sentences, but did not undo the conduct described in those cases.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump pardoned people convicted in connection with the January 6 attack on the Capitol and directed the Justice Department to seek dismissal of unresolved cases. Acting U.S. Attorney Ed Martin directed the Washington, D.C., office to file dismissal motions, including in cases involving serious assaults on police. CNN reported that the request covered more than 300 unresolved cases and that 14 members of far-right groups were released from prison early, including people convicted of seditious conspiracy.

The defendants included people convicted in attacks involving pepper spray, a stun gun, a crutch, and wooden poles. Officer Michael Fanone was among those attacked. Pardons removed criminal penalties for convicted defendants; dismissal motions sought to end pending prosecutions. Neither action erased the events or established that assault allegations were false. The clemency and dismissal directives reversed a major federal investigation and drew criticism from judges. They placed the use of executive clemency and prosecutorial discretion at the center of debate over accountability for the Capitol attack.

preserved_fields.title: DOJ Drops Charges Against Hundreds Who Violently Attacked Police on January 6
preserved_fields.description_short: DOJ Drops Charges Against Hundreds Who Violently Attacked Police on January 6
